transcript: Chapter 10 The four hounds stood in the road and did not come, and Jab stood in four feet of dead grass and let himself, for about five seconds, actually think. It was the strangest five seconds of his life. His left sleeve was filling up. His brother was making a noise behind his heels that he could not afford to listen to. There were things standing eighteen feet away that had come apart into ash under his hands and would do the same to a four-year-old in a quarter of the time. And all of that was true, and none of it was the point. And the point was this. They had not come at him. He had stepped out in front of them with the light up, and they had gone round. He had chased them right, and they had gone further right. And the one that came had not come at the boy with a burning blade. It had gone past him into the grass at the one place where there was no light at all. Huh, said Jab out loud, in a voice that did not sound like a frightened person. He put the light out to his right, slowly at the full stretch of his arm over the top of the broken frame. The whole line of them shifted left. Not much. A step and a half each, unhurried. All of them at the same speed, the way a flock of birds turns without anybody deciding. He brought the blade back across his body to the left and held it out past the bank. And they came back right, exactly as far, and stopped. And went on standing there with their heads low. Huh, said Jab. Jab, it was not a weapon to them. It had never once been a weapon to them. It was a fence. And he had spent the last four hundred paces carrying a fence around in his fist, and waving it at things, and wondering why they would not come and be cut. And behind that arriving hole the way the arithmetic always arrived, they can only come at one place. So pick it. He picked the place he was standing in. That was the part he would think about afterward, on a bench, with his hands shaking, and never managed to explain properly to anybody. The right answer was not to make himself safe. The right answer was to make the four feet he was standing in the only door in the world, and then stand in it. So he did it the other way round from every instinct in his body. He reached out to his right and laid the lit edge along the top of the broken frame, the roadside, the wide side, the side he could never have held, and he held it there, burning, an amber line four feet long lying across the way in. And he stood in the dark on the south side, with nothing in his left hand but a hole in his arm. Tonk, he said. Don't look up. The pack broke. It came all at once, the way the stillness had come. One moment four animals standing side on in a road, and the next moment four animals moving, and every one of them came at the south side. They came at him. The first one got his boot in its chest, which was not a technique either, only a leg that had been carrying a hundred and some pounds up switchbacks for sixteen days, and had a great deal of thoughtless strength left in it. It went back into the second one. The second one came over the top of it, and Jab brought the blade off the frame in a flat arc, the light guttering at the belly as it came, one breath of gutter, every single time, and cut it across the shoulders on the way through, and kept the edge moving, and got it in front of the third. Then he was down. He did not know which of them did it. Something hit him at the thigh, and the grass came up, and the wall came up, and he went into the angle with his brother's blanket under his elbow, and he got the blade out sideways and lit, and held it up and across in front of both of them like a man holding a door shut with his shoulder, and something bit down on the flat of it and came apart, and something else got past the point and took a fold of his coat and a great deal of the skin under it. Jab. Jab. Down. Stay down. He got a knee under him. He could not get the other one. He put the edge into whatever was over him, and it came off. And he put it into the next thing, and that one came off too. And he was not fighting. He had never been fighting. He was a man holding a piece of wet hide over a fire in the rain, and there were four of them and one of him. A hound came over the wing wall. It came over the coping from the north with no sound, four feet above his brother's head, and Jab saw it from underneath and knew, with the total and useless clarity of the badly outnumbered, that he was not going to get there. Then somebody hit the culvert head. He did not see it arrive. Nobody did. He found out later. That was the thing everybody said about her. There was a gray blade in the air above the coping, and a small woman on the stone behind it. And the hound that had been over the wall was going one way, and the ash of it was going another. And she had landed in the angle with her boots either side of Tonk's blanket, and was already turning. Two seconds. He counted it afterward, lying awake. And it was two seconds, and one of them was her getting up onto the wall. Which side? Somebody roared from out in the road. A man's voice big, flat, a voice built for weather. Say the side. Jab had no idea what the question meant. He answered it anyway, because his mouth was faster than the rest of him. Mine, he shouted. They come at me. They come at the dark bit. Put your light on where you don't want them. There was about a half second of nothing. You heard him! Roared the voice. Light's right. Everything lit goes right. After that, it stopped being his fight. And Jab lay in the angle of a stone wall with his brother under his arm and watched a thing he did not have the words for. A light came on out in the road. Not amber. A hard white gray. A thin cold line lying along the inner curve of something hooked. And it went right. Out to the east shoulder. And the two hounds that had been coming over the frame came off it and swung west toward the bank. Exactly the way water goes round a stone. And a big boy was standing in the bank side with his feet apart. He had no weapon of any kind. He had one arm strapped across his chest inside his coat and the other hanging. And he had planted himself in the gap between the end of the frame and the bank. In the four feet of dead grass. In front of the corner. And he simply stood there. The first hound hit him at full run. Jab watched a hundred and some pounds of it go into the boy's hip and chest at the speed of a thing that had been accelerating for thirty feet. And he braced for the boy to go down over the top of him and into his brother. The boy did not go down. He did not go back a step. He did not even get properly turned. His shoulder came round about four inches and then stopped coming round. And the hound went off him sideways into the wall and lay there scrabbling. And the second one hit him half a beat after and got exactly the same result. No, said the big boy in a completely conversational voice as if a door had blown open. Then somebody came past him on the outside faster than a person could run. And there was a crack of something like struts loading and a scatter of grit off the road. And a boy in a coat with one sleeve empty went through the space where the two hounds were getting up. And the same hooked shape was lit in his good hand. And when he had gone past there was ash in the air where they had been. He came out of it badly. His feet went from under him on the slabs at the bottom of the sag and he went down hard on the strapped arm and made a sound with a good deal in it. Torrin, I'm up. You're not up. I'm up, Dessa. Jab got himself onto his knees with his back in the corner and his arm across his brother and looked out. There were people in the road now. He could not count them. There were two lamps down and burning on the crown and a man standing in the middle of everything with his feet planted and his hands out from his sides. And the road on either side of that man had gone wrong. There was nothing to see and nothing to hear. And yet a hound went at the gap on his left and did not arrive. The way a thrown stone does not arrive when it hits a wall you have not noticed is there. The man was not a young man and he was not standing easily. His back was doing something to him. Jab could see it in the way he held his shoulders, which was not a way anybody held their shoulders on purpose. Two, said a girl's voice flat and hard from up on the bank behind them. Two left. One's in the ditch on the east, about fifteen feet down, not moving, and I don't like it. And the other? Under you? Say again? Under you, said the girl. It's in the pipe. It's under the road and it's coming west and it's about nine feet from the mouth. Jab moved before he understood the sentence. The mouth of the culvert was five feet from his own boot. It was a stone arched hole about as wide as his shoulders with black water running out of it and a dead grass fringe over the top. And he had chosen this corner and put his brother in it and never once in the whole of the last four minutes looked at the hole in the floor of it. Two sides, he had thought. Not four. Two is what there is. Three. He got his good arm under Tonk and dragged him bodily up the angle, up onto the shelf of broken stone at the back where the wing wall met the bank and got his own body down between the boy and the pipe mouth and brought the metal round and there was not enough left in him to light it. He felt it fail. It was not a refusal. There was simply nothing behind it. The way there is nothing behind a bucket. The metal sat on his fist as a fat blunt wedge with a hook on the end. The shape the light did not change. A tool for splitting fish and breaking rope and doing the eleven other jobs a person did not want to blunt a good knife on. It's dark, he said. I know, said the small woman from somewhere above and behind him. I can't. I know, she said. Mine isn't. She put herself across the mouth of the pipe with her boots in the water and her blade lit and lying flat along the stone. And the thing in the culvert came out into a grey light and did not get one whole body length out of the arch. And then it was quiet and the quiet was the strangest part of the entire night. It went from noise to nothing in about a second and a half. There was ash blowing along the road in the lamplight. A great deal of it lying in the joints between the slabs and going down the wind in long grey ropes. Somebody was coughing. Somebody a long way off was calling out a number, twice, and then a third time in a different voice, as if checking. Jab knelt in the angle of a wall with his brother against his chest and found that his arms had started to shake and that the shaking had got into his jaw and that he could not have stood up if the whole thing had started again. Four down here and one in the ditch, said the flat girl's voice. That's five. Is it five? It's five, said the big boy who did not fall over. Then that's all of them. And the last one didn't get to be the last one, which is the first time in my life I've ever seen that happen. A pause. Somebody tell Enos. Tell her yourself. I'm going to, said the girl. For years. Boy, said the man with the wrong shoulders. He had come up the road slowly and by the time Jab looked up, whatever had been on the road either side of him was not there anymore. It went out of the air the way a sound goes out of a room. And the man arrived at the culvert head with one hand out to the stone and lowered himself down onto the coping in three separate movements, like a thing being let down on a rope. How bad's the arm? It's not the arm, said Jab. Jab. The man looked at him. Then he looked at what Jab was holding and Jab watched his whole face change. And it changed the way the Carters had changed on the road that afternoon and the way the old man on the milestones had. And he understood that a certain kind of person did that everywhere and that he was going to be at the mercy of it for a while. Right, said the man. Katori. I'm here. Take the boy off him. No, said Jab. Son. No, said Jab. Nobody takes him off me. And then he looked down and the argument went out of him entirely because his brother had stopped making any noise at all. Tonk's eyes were half open and he was not looking at anything. His face had gone the color of the road. His hands, which had been shut on a cord and a wooden fish for the last five minutes and had been shut on things all his life, were open on the blanket and one of them still had the fish lying in it, not held. His skin was cold and wet at the temple and the back of the neck and hot everywhere else. His breathing had lost its rhythm. Three quick, a pause, too slow, and a pause that went on too long. Jab had seen this. He had seen it in a snow shelter fourteen nights ago by firelight with four warm stones at his brother's back. No, he said. No, no, no. Tonk. Tonk. Look at me. He's going off, said the small woman and she was already there, down on her knees in the angle with her hands going over the boy fast and professionally. Don't shake him. Get his legs up. Not that one. The other one. Get your coat under his head. That's it. How long since he ate? This morning. Half a fish. And the legs been like that how long? Seven weeks. She went still for about a quarter of a second and then went on with her hands and did not say whatever it was she had not said. Talk to him, she said. He'll come back for a voice before he comes back for anything. So Jab talked. He did not know afterward what he had said for the first part of it. He knew he had gone through the jay and the squirrel and the sitting man and that he had told him they were nearly there and that there was a stove and a doctor and a bed with a proper mattress and that his own voice had been doing something unforgivable the whole time. And none of it worked and his brother's breathing got further apart and the woman said where's that light to somebody in a voice that had changed and Jab stopped talking and put his hand flat on his brother's chest and shut his eyes. He did not push. He had learned that much in sixteen days and it had cost him an hour of a bad night and the use of his hands. Don't ask it when you want an answer. He could not stop wanting. There was no world in which he was going to stop wanting. But he could stop asking. He could let go of the reaching part, the leaning on a door part, the whole miserable business of trying to make a river run uphill. And he did. And he sat there in the ash with his hand on his brother's chest and did nothing at all. And it went out of him without asking his permission. That was the thing. It did not come when he called and it never had. It came the way his arm had come up off a gravel bar when he was thirteen years old with sixty people watching and a cold stone against his breastbone. No decision anywhere in it. Nothing of him in it except the place it came from and it went forward out of his chest into the chest that was under his hand. And it was not a blade and it had no edge and it was not any shape at all. It was warmth. It was the plainest thing in the world. Tonk's whole body jerked. Then he shuddered hard and again and the shaking came up through him from the shoulders to the heels and his hands closed one on the fish and one on a fistful of Jab's coat. And he made a small furious complaining noise into his brother's collarbone. Good, Jab said. His voice came out in pieces. That's it. Be cross. There, said the small woman very quietly at his shoulder. There he is. His breathing came up deep and ragged and regular. His color did not come back and his skin did not cool and the leg under the wrapping was exactly what it had been four minutes ago and four days ago. And Jab knew that and had known it before he started and would have done it anyway. Then the thing in his chest went out like a lamp and he found he was sitting down. He did not lose the whole of it. He lost some. There was a stretch where people moved around him and he watched them from a long way off. The way you watch rain while you're asleep. Somebody put a coat over his shoulders. Somebody got his left sleeve cut off at the elbow and wound something round the forearm very tight and he did not care for that but could not raise a convincing objection. Somebody put a hand under his jaw and turned his face toward a lamp and said he's not with us and somebody else said he's with us. He's just done which he thought was about right and would have said so if he could. The next thing he was properly inside was a girl crouched in front of him with a lamp held low. She was about 13 with a scar over one ear where no hair grew and she was not looking at him at all. She was looking at the ground between them and at the wall and at the ash in the joints of the slabs and at the marks his own boots had made in the dead grass. She had come from somewhere off to the east. There was frost and ditch mud all up the side of her from the knee down. You went down on your left knee there she said. And then you got up and went right and then you fell over your own frame. Yes said Jab. Why'd you go right? Because they went right. They went right because of the light she said. And it was not a question and she said it the way a person says a thing they have already worked out and once checked. You had it out on that side and they went off it. Yes. How long have you known that? Jab thought about it. It seemed important to be accurate. About four minutes he said. The girl looked up at him for the first time. She had a very direct sort of face. Right she said. That's faster than me. She stood up and turned round and pointed the lamp down the road south toward the knot of yellow light in the sag and the low black line of the berm beyond it. Don't go down the middle. The whole crown slabs and half of them rock and you'll have him off a stretcher in fifty yards. Go along the east shoulder to the second lamp and then cut up onto the road where the ditch shallows. There's nine feet of good hard verge there and then it's made surface all the way to the gate. It's three hundred and forty paces. I've walked it. I can carry him. You can't carry anything said the girl. I've carried him four hundred miles. She looked at him for a moment. Then you'll walk beside him she said and you'll hold his hand and that's the same thing and it weighs less. She put two fingers in her mouth and whistled up the road and it was the loudest noise anybody had made all night. Otto bring the barrow. bring the barrow. Bring the barrow. the barrow. Go to town. Give the barrow. We'll talk Thank you.
